processing: White tea picked under an 'untouched by human hand' rule, meant to keep sweat, skin and metal away from the leaf, then handled gently in the small quantities typical of bud white tea.
harvest_season: Very low yield: Handunugoda pluckers are reported to gather only about 160 grams a day, against about 30 kilos in ordinary plucking. No prized season is documented.
appearance_dry: Typically small, pale, downy buds in silver-grey, as with other bud-only white teas.
appearance_liquor: Typically very pale straw and clear, as with other bud-only white teas.
appearance_wet: Typically soft, intact, pale green buds.
taste_profile: Little is documented about its taste; as with other bud-only white teas, expect a light, sweet and softly floral cup.

brewing.notes: General guidance for bud-only white tea. Use cooler water and do not rinse: there is too little leaf to waste.

vintage_note: Handunugoda's Herman Virgin White was reported at only about 10 kilos a year, so it reaches buyers in tiny lots through very few sellers. Harvest years are rarely publicised, and as with other bud whites it should be drunk fresh; ask for the year.
description:
Virgin White Tea is a Sri Lankan white tea defined less by a taste than by a picking rule: the leaf should not be touched by bare human hands. The best-known version is Herman Virgin White from the Handunugoda estate, and Weligama in the south is the area linked with it.

The yield is what makes it extreme. Handunugoda's pluckers are reported to gather about 160 grams a day, compared with about 30 kilos for ordinary plucking, and the estate's yearly output was put at around 10 kilos.

Little has been written about how it actually tastes. As with other bud-only whites, it should be light and gently sweet, so brew with cooler water and pay attention, as a strong tea this is not.

The price is the headline: one trade report gave US$1,500 a kilo, and it counts among the costliest teas sold. You are paying for rarity and the method as much as for the cup, and the term is not a protected one. Check for the estate name, and try a good Ceylon silver tips first for comparison.
history:
The name borrows from a Chinese legend of imperial tribute tea, in which young virgins wearing gold gloves cut the leaf at dawn with gold scissors and laid it in gold baskets. Treat this as a story, though its practical logic is plain enough: keep the leaf away from anything that could taint it.

The Sri Lankan tea is a deliberate modern throwback to that idea, with the 'untouched' rule kept and the rule about the pickers dropped. Handunugoda's version became known through its extreme yield and price. When production began is not clearly documented.
